fast-transformer-decoding-one-write-head.oneSentence: Multi-query attention keeps many query heads but shares a single key/value head across them, slashing the memory bandwidth of autoregressive decoding at only minor quality cost.
fast-transformer-decoding-one-write-head.summary: Shazeer diagnoses why Transformer decoding is slow — every autoregressive step reloads the full per-head key and value tensors, making incremental generation memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound — and fixes it by sharing one set of keys and values across all attention heads (multi-query attention). For this curriculum the paper is the conceptual seed of the grouped-query attention you hand-write in Phase 3: MQA is simply the n_kv_head=1 extreme of the n_kv_head knob, and the KV-cache savings it motivates are exactly what you measure when you get to inference engineering in Phase 6.
coreIdeas: Training attention is cheap because sequence length is parallel; decoding is expensive because it is sequential and reloads the growing K/V cache every step, so decode is memory-bandwidth bound.
Sharing keys and values across heads (keeping only the query heads distinct) divides the offending memory-to-compute term by the number of heads h, giving Theta(1/d + n/(d*h) + 1/b).
Query-side head diversity matters far more than key/value-side diversity: MQA loses far less quality than simply reducing the number of heads for the same savings.
The payoff is decode speed, not train speed: >12x faster incremental decoding (46 -> 3.8 us/token) for a tiny quality cost (BLEU 26.7 -> 26.5).
fast-transformer-decoding-one-write-head.whyItMatters: This paper turns 'attention' from a single fixed block into a design space with a bandwidth-versus-quality tradeoff. It is the direct ancestor of grouped-query attention and the reason modern LLMs use fewer key/value heads than query heads to keep the KV cache small during generation.
fast-transformer-decoding-one-write-head.phaseConnection: Phase 3 architecture ablations: you implement grouped-query attention with an n_kv_head knob, and MQA is the n_kv_head=1 endpoint — read this for the mechanism and the memory-bandwidth reasoning behind the knob. The measured payoff (smaller KV cache, faster decode) is what you actually quantify later in Phase 6 inference engineering.
suggestedReadingFocus: Which tensors keep the head dimension (Q, P_q, P_o) versus lose it (K, V, P_k, P_v) under multi-query attention.
The incremental performance analysis in Sections 2.4 and 3.1 — how the n/d memory term arises and how head-sharing divides it by h.
Table 1 versus Table 2: MQA's small quality drop against its large decode-speed win, and why it beats naively reducing the head count.

gqa-training-generalized-multi-query-tra.oneSentence: Grouped-query attention gives each group of query heads a single shared key/value head, dialing between multi-head and multi-query attention to shrink the KV cache while keeping near-multi-head quality.
gqa-training-generalized-multi-query-tra.summary: GQA adds one knob to attention: the number of key/value heads, expressed as G groups of query heads that each share a KV head (GQA-1 is multi-query attention, GQA-H is multi-head attention). Shrinking the KV heads leaves query capacity intact, so quality barely moves while the KV cache — and the memory bandwidth that dominates autoregressive decoding — shrinks by a factor of H/G. On uptrained T5-XXL, GQA-8 matches multi-head quality (average 47.1 vs 47.2) at roughly 5x faster inference (0.28s vs 1.51s per sample). The paper also gives a cheap way to obtain such a model without pre-training from scratch: mean-pool an existing multi-head checkpoint's KV projections into the reduced structure, then continue pre-training for only ~5% of the original steps.
coreIdeas: Autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound: every step reloads the KV cache, so the number of key/value heads — not query heads or attention FLOPs — is what governs decode speed.
GQA interpolates between MQA (one KV head) and MHA (one KV head per query head) with G groups; the KV cache and data loaded per step shrink by exactly H/G = n_head / n_kv_head.

Because GQA removes redundant KV heads rather than query capacity, model quality is nearly unchanged (GQA-8 ties MHA) while inference gets far cheaper — the win lives at inference time, not in the training loss.

You can convert an existing MHA checkpoint by mean-pooling its per-head KV projections (better than picking one head or random init) and uptraining for a small proportion alpha=0.05 of the original steps.

GQA scales better than MQA: KV cache grows linearly with model dimension while params/FLOPs grow quadratically, and it avoids the sharding waste of replicating a single MQA KV head across partitions; it is also more training-stable than MQA.
gqa-training-generalized-multi-query-tra.whyItMatters: GQA is the reason the Microlab GQAAttention module has an n_kv_head knob, and this paper explains why turning that knob barely moves the loss: it prunes duplicated key/value heads, not the query capacity that drives quality. That is exactly what the Phase 3 architecture ablation finds — a change that looks nearly free at training time. The payoff is deliberately invisible here and only becomes measurable in Phase 6 (inference engineering), where the KV cache, and thus decode latency and memory, shrinks by n_head / n_kv_head. It is a clean lesson that some architecture choices are justified by the inference regime, not the training curve.
gqa-training-generalized-multi-query-tra.phaseConnection: Phase 3 (architecture ablations): hand-write GQAAttention with an n_kv_head knob and confirm the paper's core claim — sweeping n_kv_head from n_head (MHA) down toward 1 (MQA) barely changes validation loss. Set n_kv_head at construction time (the from-scratch analogue of the paper's mean-pool-and-uptrain conversion), and carry the same knob forward so Phase 6 can measure the KV-cache reduction of n_head / n_kv_head that motivates GQA. The Llama 3 reading uses GQA for this reason, so this paper is the mechanism behind an architecture choice the learner sees adopted in a production decoder-only model.
suggestedReadingFocus: How the number of key/value heads (groups G) maps to KV-cache size and to memory bandwidth in autoregressive decoding
Why quality stays near multi-head while speed approaches multi-query — the query-capacity-vs-KV-redundancy distinction
The mean-pooling checkpoint conversion and alpha=0.05 uptraining recipe, and how a from-scratch decoder-only build simply sets n_kv_head instead
The scaling and sharding arguments (Section 2.2) plus the decoder-only remark in the Limitations that connect this T5 result to Llama-style models

extending-context-window-of-large-langua.oneSentence: Position Interpolation extends a RoPE model's context window by dividing position indices by the scale factor so they land back inside the pre-trained range, recovering good perplexity after only a short fine-tune where naive extrapolation fails catastrophically.
extending-context-window-of-large-langua.summary: This is the paper behind your Phase 8 continued-pretraining exercise. RoPE-based models like LLaMA are pre-trained at a fixed window (2048) and extrapolate terribly, so feeding longer sequences sends perplexity above 10^3. Position Interpolation fixes it with one idea: rescale every position index by L/L' so the maximum index — and thus the maximum relative distance RoPE ever sees — stays inside the trained range, replacing f(x, m) with f(x, mL/L'). RoPE's attention score is smooth between trained integer positions but explodes beyond them, so interpolating is provably far more stable (Theorem 2.1 gives a ~600x smaller error bound). In this phase you hand-write `interpolated_rope_cache` by dividing positions by the scale, then extend your own 150M model's block from 1024 to 2048 — a scale factor of 2, i.e. positions divided by 2. You reproduce the paper's exact three-stage arc on your own model: perplexity raw (bad — direct extrapolation blows up, like the paper's >10^3), then with interpolation applied (better — usable immediately at zero training, mirroring the paper's step-0 perplexity of 16.10 for 7B at 8192), then after a short fine-tune (best — dropping below the original window's baseline, as the paper's 6.95 beats its own 7.20 at 2048).
coreIdeas: Extend the window by down-scaling position indices (divide by the scale factor L'/L) so RoPE is only ever evaluated inside its trained range, instead of extrapolating past it.
Interpolation is stable because RoPE's attention score is smooth between trained integer positions, whereas extrapolation is unbounded and catastrophic — a ~600x difference in the error bound.
A very short fine-tune (~1000 steps, insensitive to the data) is enough because the model is only adapting to a reshaped position range, not learning new knowledge.
extending-context-window-of-large-langua.whyItMatters: It converts an expensive problem — training a long-context model from scratch — into a cheap, parameter-free rescaling plus a brief finetune. It is the canonical, minimal context-extension method and the conceptual root of later scalings (NTK-aware, YaRN) you will meet after this phase.
extending-context-window-of-large-langua.phaseConnection: Phase 8 (continued pretraining): you hand-write `interpolated_rope_cache` (positions divided by scale) and extend your 150M model from block 1024 to 2048, measuring perplexity raw (bad) then interpolated (better) then after a short finetune (best) — a direct, small-scale replay of Table 3.
suggestedReadingFocus: Eqn 4, f'(x, m) = f(x, mL/L') — map 'divide positions by the scale factor' to your 1024-to-2048 case (scale 2, positions divided by 2).
Section 2.2 and Figure 2 — why extrapolation explodes but interpolation stays smooth, the reason your raw-vs-interpolated perplexity gap is so large.
Table 3 — the raw / interpolation-only / fine-tuned perplexity progression you are reproducing on your own model.

tensor-programs-v-tuning-large-neural-ne.oneSentence: The Maximal Update Parametrization (muP) makes a model's optimal hyperparameters stable across width, so you can tune a cheap narrow proxy and copy the learning rate and multipliers zero-shot to the full-size model.
tensor-programs-v-tuning-large-neural-ne.summary: This paper converts infinite-width theory into a concrete tuning recipe: scale each parameter tensor's initialization, learning rate, and output multiplier by the right power of width so that every layer's activations update by a width-independent amount. Once a model is written in muP, its best learning rate stops drifting with size, so hyperparameters found on a small proxy transfer to a large target without a full-scale sweep (muTransfer). The practical core is a small multiplier table — hidden-weight init variance ~ 1/fan_in (std ~ 1/sqrt(width)), hidden-weight Adam LR ~ 1/width, an output-logit multiplier ~ 1/width, and 1/d attention — plus a coordinate check that confirms the implementation by keeping every activation's coordinate size flat across widths.
coreIdeas: In the standard parametrization the optimal learning rate shifts with width, so a small model's tuned HPs are wrong for a large one; muP re-scales per-layer init/LR/multipliers so the optimum stays put.

The recipe is a compact table over three parameter classes (input weights & biases, output weights, hidden weights): the load-bearing rules are hidden init var ~ 1/fan_in, hidden Adam LR ~ 1/width, an output multiplier ~ 1/width, and 1/d attention.
muTransfer (Algorithm 1): parametrize the target in muP, tune a narrow proxy, copy the HPs zero-shot — validated up to GPT-3 6.7B tuned from a 40M proxy at 7% of pretraining cost.
A coordinate check verifies correctness: over a few training steps across a wide width range, every activation's average coordinate size should stay Theta(1); blow-up or shrinkage flags a bug.
Optimization HPs, initialization, and multipliers transfer (across width, and empirically depth/batch/seqlen/steps); regularization HPs like dropout and weight decay do not.
tensor-programs-v-tuning-large-neural-ne.whyItMatters: This is the paper that makes the Phase 4 scaling experiments affordable: instead of an unaffordable learning-rate sweep on the 1B capstone, you tune a small proxy and transfer the LR by muP. Hand-writing the muP multiplier table (hidden LR ~ 1/m, hidden init ~ 1/sqrt(m), output mult ~ 1/m, 1/d attention) turns the abstract rules into the exact code changes your model needs.
tensor-programs-v-tuning-large-neural-ne.phaseConnection: Use it directly in Phase 4: write the muP multiplier table for your Transformer, retrofit 1/d attention and the per-layer init/LR/multiplier scalings, then run a coordinate check across widths to confirm every activation stays Theta(1) before trusting the transfer. Pick the 1B capstone's learning rate by transferring from a narrow proxy rather than sweeping the full model, and remember to tune only optimization/init/multiplier HPs on the proxy, not regularization.
suggestedReadingFocus: Table 3 and the equivalent Table 8 — the muP multiplier table you will hand-write, and the unifying '1/fan_in multiplier for any weight mapping an infinite dimension to a finite one' interpretation
Definition 4.1 and Appendix B.1 — 1/d attention and the concrete per-tensor Transformer walkthrough
Appendix D.1 and Figure 5 — the coordinate check as the correctness test for your implementation
Table 1 and Section 6.1 — which HPs transfer, across which dimensions, and the minimum-scale caveats

small-scale-proxies-for-large-scale-tran.oneSentence: Wortsman et al. show that large-model training instabilities can be reproduced, mitigated, and even predicted in small Transformers by training at high learning rate and tracking LR-vs-loss curves and activation/gradient norms.
small-scale-proxies-for-large-scale-tran.summary: This paper is loss-spike literacy in one place, and it maps almost exactly onto this lab's situation: study the failures on small proxies, then carry the lessons into a bigger run. The authors reproduce two instabilities that were first reported only at enormous scale. Attention-logit growth is when the pre-softmax logits z_ij = <q_i,k_j>/sqrt(d_h) blow up, the softmax saturates, and attention collapses toward one-hot; you see it as the max attention logit (worst in layer 0) climbing toward ~1e4 early in training, and qk-layernorm — LayerNorm on the queries and keys before the logits — mitigates it. Output-logit divergence is when the softmax normalizer log Z (and the output-logit mean) drifts strongly negative late in training; an auxiliary z-loss = log^2(Z) at coefficient 1e-4 keeps log Z near zero and mitigates it. The unifying tool is the LR-vs-loss curve summarized by LR sensitivity (expected deviation from optimal loss when the learning rate is swept across ~3 orders of magnitude). The key scaling lesson: instabilities show up as the loss exploding at high LR, and the learning rate at which a model diverges shrinks as scale grows — the stable LR window narrows, so an LR that was safe at 150M can diverge at 1B. Crucially, all of this reproduces at just a few million parameters, and the instabilities can be forecast before they emerge from the scaling behavior of internal norms.
coreIdeas: Attention-logit growth: z_ij = <q_i,k_j>/sqrt(d_h) grows large, the softmax saturates and attention collapses to near one-hot; symptom is max attention logit climbing toward ~1e4 (worst in layer 0) early in training; mitigation is qk-layernorm (LayerNorm on q and k before the logits).

Output-logit divergence: with p_i = e^{y_i}/Z, the normalizer log Z (output-logit mean) drifts strongly negative late in training; mitigation is z-loss = log^2(Z) at coefficient 1e-4, keeping log Z near zero (weight decay also helps at larger scale).

LR sensitivity summarizes an LR-vs-loss curve as one number, the expected deviation from optimal loss over a ~3-orders-of-magnitude LR sweep; it rises with scale even with qk-layernorm, and instability appears as loss exploding at high LR while the divergence LR shrinks with scale (the stable window narrows).

Instabilities are predictable before they diverge: a quadratic fit to max-attention-logit-vs-scale forecast a 4.8B model would diverge at LR 1e-2 (confirmed), and gradient RMS falling toward the default AdamW epsilon (1e-8) flags that updates Delta = v/(sqrt(u)+epsilon) will shrink and parameters will stop learning unless epsilon is lowered.

Other stability levers reshape the same curves: longer warm-up and independent/decoupled weight decay reduce LR sensitivity, scaling depth raises it faster than width, and muParam stabilizes the optimal LR across width without improving loss.
small-scale-proxies-for-large-scale-tran.whyItMatters: This is the practitioner's manual for not wasting a large pretraining run on a preventable divergence. It names the two failure modes by their telemetry (max attention logit, log Z / output-logit mean, gradient RMS), gives cheap code-level mitigations (qk-layernorm, z-loss, longer warm-up, decoupled weight decay, a smaller AdamW epsilon), and — most valuably — shows you can predict instability from small proxy runs instead of discovering it after burning the compute.
small-scale-proxies-for-large-scale-tran.phaseConnection: Phase 4 reading, immediately before the largest pretraining run in the lab (a 1B model). Add qk-layernorm and z-loss to the training code, and instrument the run to log max attention logit, log Z / output-logit mean, and per-layer gradient RMS. Do a short LR sweep on a smaller proxy first — because the stable LR window narrows with scale, an LR that worked at 150M may diverge at 1B — and extrapolate the attention-logit and gradient-RMS trends to sanity-check the 1B run before launching it. This paper is the lab's own situation stated as method: small proxies for large-scale stability.
suggestedReadingFocus: The two instabilities as symptoms to monitor: what attention-logit growth vs output-logit divergence look like in the telemetry, and when in training each appears.
qk-layernorm and z-loss as concrete implementation changes, plus the secondary levers (warm-up length, independent/decoupled weight decay, AdamW epsilon).
LR sensitivity and how LR-vs-loss curves shift with scale — the mechanism behind the narrowing stable learning-rate window.
The prediction results (max-attention-logit quadratic fit; gradient-RMS approaching AdamW epsilon) as a recipe for forecasting stability of the 1B run from cheaper proxy runs.

eliciting-latent-predictions-from-transf.oneSentence: The tuned lens replaces the fragile, biased logit lens with a learned per-layer affine probe, giving trustworthy layer-by-layer readouts of what a transformer 'thinks' the next token is.
eliciting-latent-predictions-from-transf.summary: This is the rigorous companion to the plain logit lens you hand-write in this phase. You decode every layer's residual stream through your model's own final norm and unembedding, LayerNorm[h_l] W_U, and watch the prediction trajectory sharpen toward the answer. Belrose et al. show why that naive lens is not to be trusted: it is unreliable (it breaks on whole model families, often just echoing the input token), it is a biased estimator of the true output (several bits of KL on the marginal distribution), and it ignores representational drift — the residual-stream basis rotates with depth, so zeroing out the later layers feeds an off-distribution vector into the unembedding. The fix is a tuned lens: for each layer, learn a small affine 'translator' A_l h_l + b_l (a d_model x d_model matrix plus bias) that re-aligns the hidden state before it hits the frozen unembedding, trained by KL-distilling against the model's own final logits. The unembedding stays frozen, so the probe is cheap and cannot smuggle in information the model never computed.
coreIdeas: The plain logit lens is early exiting: it zeroes every residual update after layer l, which is arbitrary and off-distribution because hidden-state covariance drifts across depth and the network may lean on the summed residuals as a bias term.

The logit lens is provably biased and often unreliable — measure it as the KL divergence between the true and lens marginals, which can be 4-5 bits per layer, versus 0.0068 bits between two well-matched final distributions.
The tuned lens learns one affine translator (A_l, b_l) per layer and composes it with the model's frozen unembedding: TunedLens_l(h_l) = LayerNorm[A_l h_l + b_l] W_U.

Translators are trained by distillation — minimize KL(model's final logits || tuned-lens logits) — using the model's own output as a soft target so the probe never learns information the model didn't actually compute.

Freezing the unembedding makes each probe just d_model x d_model instead of |V| x d_model; the whole lens trains in under an hour and its directions are causally faithful to the model (Spearman 0.89).
eliciting-latent-predictions-from-transf.whyItMatters: It is the difference between a demo and a measurement. Your from-scratch logit lens will produce pretty pictures on your 150M model, but this paper explains why you cannot read those pictures as the model's actual beliefs, and gives a concrete, cheap correction that makes them trustworthy. It also sets the interpretability standard for the whole phase: a per-layer readout is only meaningful if it is unbiased AND causally reflects the computation the model performs, which the paper operationalizes with distillation losses and causal basis extraction.
eliciting-latent-predictions-from-transf.phaseConnection: Read it right after you have your hand-written logit lens running on your 150M model. First reproduce the failure modes it describes — plot your model's per-layer bias (KL of the marginals) and look for layers where top-1 just echoes the input token. Then extend the lens you already wrote: add a d_model x d_model translator plus bias per layer, initialize to the identity, freeze your unembedding, and train the translators by KL-distilling against your model's own final logits on a validation slice. Compare the tuned trajectory's per-layer perplexity and bias against the plain lens to confirm you have measured, not just visualized, the model's latent predictions.
suggestedReadingFocus: The two formulas side by side — LayerNorm[h_l] W_U versus LayerNorm[A_l h_l + b_l] W_U — and exactly what each learned term (A_l, b_l) corrects.
How bias is defined and measured (KL between the true and lens marginal distributions) and why a predictable bias breaks the belief-updating interpretation.
The distillation loss (Eq. 9) and why the target is the model's own final logits rather than ground-truth next tokens.
Why freezing the unembedding (d_model x d_model translator, not |V| x d_model) is what makes the method cheap enough to train on your own model in under an hour.

locating-and-editing-factual-association.oneSentence: Meng et al. locate factual associations in GPT with causal tracing — mid-layer MLPs at the last subject token — then prove the location is causal by inserting new facts with a closed-form rank-one weight edit (ROME).
locating-and-editing-factual-association.summary: This paper is the canonical 'locate then intervene' study of mechanistic interpretability, and it is the natural next rung above the logit-lens and induction-head analysis you are already doing on your 150M model. Part one, Causal Tracing, runs the network three times on a factual prompt — clean, subject-corrupted, and corrupted-with-a-single-clean-state-restored — and measures which lone hidden state can RESTORE the correct answer. Averaged over 1000 facts, this reveals that mid-layer MLPs processing the LAST subject token are decisive; severing MLP computation there kills the effect, so the localization is causal, not correlational. Part two, ROME, tests that finding by editing: it treats the MLP down-projection W_proj as a linear associative memory (a key-value store) and derives a closed-form rank-one update, W_hat = W + Lambda(C^-1 k*)^T, that maps a subject key k* to a new value v* while a pre-cached key covariance C minimizes collateral damage to other stored facts. On the CounterFact dataset, ROME uniquely achieves both generalization (the edit survives paraphrasing) and specificity (neighboring subjects stay untouched), where fine-tuning and hypernetworks each sacrifice one. Crucially, sweeping the edit across layers and tokens reproduces the tracing map — locate, intervene, then confirm.
coreIdeas: Causal Tracing localizes a fact by noising the subject to erase it, then restoring one hidden state at a time and measuring the Indirect Effect — the recovery of the correct-answer probability attributable to that single state.
Facts in GPT live at an 'early site': mid-layer MLP modules processing the last token of the subject, distinct from the expected 'late site' where attention assembles the final prediction.
An MLP behaves as a linear associative (key-value) memory — W_fc encodes a subject key, W_proj retrieves the value — which is exactly what makes a single-shot, no-retraining weight edit possible.

ROME inserts a fact with a closed-form rank-one update W_hat = W + Lambda(C^-1 k*)^T, choosing the subject key k* by averaging over prefixed contexts and the value v* by optimizing for the target object while preserving the subject's essence.

The right editing test separates generalization (edit survives rephrasing) from specificity (neighbors unchanged); ROME achieves both at once, and the best edit location independently confirms the causal-tracing result.
locating-and-editing-factual-association.whyItMatters: It upgrades your interpretability toolkit from reading representations to proving them: logit lens and induction heads tell you what a component seems to represent, but causal tracing tells you what a component causally DOES, by ablating and restoring it. That locate-then-intervene discipline — and the finding that mid-layer MLPs act as key-value fact stores — is a lens you can point directly at your own from-scratch 150M model.
locating-and-editing-factual-association.phaseConnection: Phase 5 (interpretability): you are already running logit-lens and induction-head analysis by hand. ROME is the next level — apply causal tracing to find where a fact lives in your model's mid-layer MLPs, then use a rank-one edit to prove that location is causal rather than merely correlated. The takeaway to carry forward is the methodology itself: locate with an intervention, intervene to prove it, then confirm the two agree.
suggestedReadingFocus: The three-run Causal Tracing protocol (clean / corrupted / corrupted-with-restoration) and the Indirect Effect it computes — the rigorous cousin of the logit-lens probing you already do.
Why mid-layer MLPs at the last subject token are the causal store, and how severing MLP computation proves it rather than merely correlating with it.
The MLP-as-key-value-memory framing and ROME's rank-one update term by term (k*, v*, the covariance C, and Lambda).
The generalization-versus-specificity evaluation on CounterFact, and how the layer/token editing sweep reproduces the tracing map to close the locate-then-intervene loop.

efficient-memory-management-for-large-la.oneSentence: PagedAttention stores each request's KV cache in fixed-size, non-contiguous blocks addressed through an OS-style block table, eliminating the fragmentation and over-reservation of contiguous caches so vLLM can batch far more requests and serve LLMs at 2-4x higher throughput.
efficient-memory-management-for-large-la.summary: Kwon et al. show LLM serving is memory-bound: the KV cache grows unpredictably per request, yet existing systems pre-allocate a single contiguous chunk sized to the maximum sequence length, so only 20.4-38.2% of that memory ever holds real tokens -- the rest lost to reserved slots, internal fragmentation, and external fragmentation. PagedAttention reinterprets OS virtual-memory paging: it splits each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens) that need not be contiguous, mapped logical-to-physical by a per-request block table and allocated one block at a time on demand. This drops KV waste to near zero (96.3% utilization), and a block reference count with copy-on-write lets sequences share prompt and prefix blocks for parallel sampling and beam search. Freed of max-length reservation, vLLM can run continuous (iteration-level) batching over many more requests, delivering 2-4x the throughput of FasterTransformer and Orca at equal latency.
coreIdeas: LLM serving is memory-bound; the KV cache -- dynamic, per-request, and unknown in length a priori -- is what caps the batch size and therefore throughput.
Contiguous max-length pre-allocation wastes most KV memory to reserved slots plus internal and external fragmentation, leaving only ~20-38% for actual token state.
Paging the KV cache into fixed-size non-contiguous blocks with a logical-to-physical block table confines waste to at most one partially filled block per sequence.
Block-level indirection with reference counting and copy-on-write enables KV sharing across sequences (parallel sampling, beam search, shared prefixes) that a contiguous cache cannot offer.
Removing max-length reservation is what lets continuous batching pack many more requests per step, yielding 2-4x throughput -- largest for long sequences, big models, and complex decoding.
efficient-memory-management-for-large-la.whyItMatters: This is the exact upgrade path for the naive contiguous, preallocated KV cache the learner just hand-wrote for their 150M model. The paper names, one by one, the wastes that cache suffers -- reserved future slots, over-provisioned tails, allocator gaps -- and shows the block-table data structure that fixes them. It is the canonical inference-engineering paper for turning a single-request toy cache into a serving-scale memory manager, and the foundation of vLLM.
efficient-memory-management-for-large-la.phaseConnection: Phase 6 (inference engineering) reading, taken up right after hand-writing the naive KV cache. Use it to redesign that cache as paged blocks with a block table, then build toward continuous batching: the paper motivates why the flat preallocated tensor caps batch size, and PagedAttention is the concrete virtual-memory-style structure the learner reimplements at a smaller scale.
suggestedReadingFocus: Map Sec 3.1's three memory wastes directly onto the learner's naive contiguous KV cache -- each waste is a concrete bug to remove.
The block table (Sec 4.2): the logical-to-physical mapping and on-demand block allocation are the data structure to implement in place of a flat max-length tensor.
Why attention must be rewritten block-wise (Eq 4) once KV lives in scattered blocks -- a paged cache is useless unless the kernel can gather from non-contiguous blocks.
Copy-on-write with reference counts (Sec 4.4) and how continuous batching (Sec 2.3, 4.5) becomes possible once max-length reservation is gone.

fast-inference-from-transformers-via-spe.oneSentence: Speculative decoding makes a large Transformer generate 2X-3X faster by letting a small draft model guess several tokens ahead and verifying them in one parallel pass of the large model, using an accept/reject rule that provably leaves the target's output distribution unchanged.
fast-inference-from-transformers-via-spe.summary: Autoregressive decoding is slow because K tokens need K serial runs of the model, and a single large-model step is memory-bandwidth bound, leaving arithmetic capacity idle. Speculative decoding spends that idle compute: a cheap draft model M_q proposes gamma tokens, the target model M_p scores all gamma+1 positions in one parallel forward pass, and a speculative sampling rule accepts the longest run of guesses that is consistent with an exact draw from the target. The rule is small and exact — accept each draft token with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft), and resample any rejection from normalize(max(0, p_target - p_draft)). A short algebra argument shows the emitted token is distributed exactly as p_target, so the method changes latency without changing what the model would have sampled. This is the centerpiece the learner reconstructs by hand in Phase 6: the rule, and the proof of why it is lossless.
coreIdeas: A small draft model proposes gamma tokens; the large target model verifies all of them in a single parallel forward pass, so one target call can emit up to gamma+1 tokens and always at least one.

The accept/reject rule is exact: accept a draft token with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft) and resample rejections from normalize(max(0, p_target - p_draft)); the emitted distribution equals p_target for every token.

The acceptance rate alpha = E(min(p_target, p_draft)) sets the speedup via E(tokens/step) = (1 - alpha^(gamma+1))/(1 - alpha); a better draft (higher alpha) means more accepted tokens per target call.

It trades extra arithmetic for fewer memory accesses (target weights and KV cache read once per step, not per token), so it only wins in the common bandwidth-bound decode regime — and any draft model works, with correctness never at risk.
fast-inference-from-transformers-via-spe.whyItMatters: This is the anchor paper for Phase 6 (inference engineering): the learner hand-writes the accept/reject rule and, crucially, proves WHY it samples from the target distribution unchanged rather than treating it as a heuristic. That proof — P(x) = min(p_target, p_draft) + max(0, p_target - p_draft) = p_target — is the difference between an approximation that quietly corrupts outputs (the kind of masked bug this lab avoids) and a lossless speedup. It also teaches the compute-vs-bandwidth trade-off that governs all real LLM serving: you can only cash in spare FLOPs for latency when decode is memory-bound.
fast-inference-from-transformers-via-spe.phaseConnection: In Phase 6 you implement the speculative decoding step end to end: draft gamma tokens from a small model, run the target once over all positions, compute n accepted guesses from the ratio p_target/p_draft against uniform draws, and emit the corrected token from normalize(max(0, p_target - p_draft)) — then verify empirically that outputs match plain sampling from the target. The forward connection is to Phase 14 (distillation): the paper proves ANY draft works and that speedup scales with alpha = E(min(p_target, p_draft)), and a distilled student is trained precisely to match its teacher's distribution — so your Phase 14 student is a purpose-built, high-alpha draft model, closing the loop between distillation and fast inference.
suggestedReadingFocus: The accept/reject rule in Section 2.3 and Algorithm 1 — the exact formulas you will reimplement in Phase 6.
The Appendix A.1 correctness argument: reconstruct why P(output = x) collapses to p_target(x), so you can defend that the speedup is lossless.
alpha = E(min(p,q)) and E(tokens/step) = (1 - alpha^(gamma+1))/(1 - alpha), which quantify how draft quality (and later, distillation quality) turns into speedup.
Sections 3.3-3.4 on the wall-time vs arithmetic-operations trade-off and why memory bandwidth being the bottleneck is what makes the method pay off.

gptq-accurate-post-training-quantization.oneSentence: GPTQ quantizes large Transformer weights to 3-4 bits in one shot by using approximate second-order (Hessian) information to compensate rounding error column by column, where naive round-to-nearest falls apart.
gptq-accurate-post-training-quantization.summary: GPTQ is the smart cousin of the round-to-nearest quantizer you hand-write in Phase 6. Instead of rounding each weight to the nearest grid point independently, it solves a per-layer reconstruction problem — minimize the change to the layer's *output* on a little calibration data — by quantizing one column at a time and using the inverse layer Hessian to nudge the remaining weights so they absorb the error just introduced. Three engineering moves (share one inverse Hessian across all rows via a fixed column order, batch updates over blocks of 128 columns to beat the memory-bandwidth wall, and a Cholesky reformulation with mild dampening for numerical stability) scale an idea that previously topped out near 100M parameters up to 175B in about four GPU hours. The payoff is exactly the gap RTN leaves open: 3-4 bit weights with negligible perplexity loss, plus a memory-bound dequantize-on-the-fly kernel that turns the smaller footprint into real per-token speedups.
coreIdeas: Quantize to minimize the layer's output error on calibration activations (argmin ||WX - WhatX||^2), not the per-weight rounding error — this is what lets one weight's larger error be paid for by adjusting the others.

After quantizing each column, use the inverse layer Hessian H = 2XX^T to push the not-yet-quantized weights so the output barely moves; this second-order error compensation is why 3-4 bit survives where RTN collapses.

Scale is an engineering problem: a shared arbitrary column order kills the cubic compute, lazy block updates kill the memory-bandwidth stall, and a Cholesky reformulation kills the numerical blow-up at billion-parameter scale.

The inference win is memory-bound — a dequantize-on-the-fly kernel moving fewer bytes, not faster arithmetic — so it speeds up autoregressive decoding, which is dominated by memory-bound matrix-vector products.
gptq-accurate-post-training-quantization.whyItMatters: Phase 6 has you hand-write naive groupwise absmax round-to-nearest quantization and measure its perplexity cost on your 150M model. GPTQ is the principled version of that same baseline: it shows exactly why RTN degrades and how second-order error compensation recovers most of the loss, making 3-4 bit practical. It is also a clean case study in the recurring inference-engineering lesson that latency is set by bytes moved, not FLOPs.
gptq-accurate-post-training-quantization.phaseConnection: Read it right after your Phase 6 RTN exercise: treat the OPT WikiText2 table as the gap between your hand-written baseline and the state of the art, and note that grouping (which your RTN already uses) stacks on top of GPTQ. It sets up the rest of the inference phase — KV-cache sizing, memory-bandwidth-bound decoding, and custom low-bit kernels.
suggestedReadingFocus: The layer-wise objective ||WX - WhatX||^2 and why minimizing output error beats independent rounding
The error-compensation step: how the inverse Hessian decides how much to nudge the surviving weights (OBQ Equations 2-3)
The three scaling tricks (shared order, lazy batching, Cholesky) and which bottleneck each one removes
Why the speedup is memory-bound and gets no faster arithmetic, and how that maps onto autoregressive decoding

megatron-lm-training-multi-billion-param.oneSentence: Megatron-LM splits each transformer layer's matrix multiplies across GPUs — tensor (intra-layer) model parallelism — so multi-billion-parameter models fit in aggregate GPU memory with only two all-reduces per forward pass.
megatron-lm-training-multi-billion-param.summary: Megatron-LM is the origin of the tensor-parallel (tp) idea this phase is built around. Instead of assigning whole layers to GPUs, it partitions the two big GEMMs inside every transformer block: the MLP is split column-then-row so the nonlinear GeLU applies per-partition with no communication, and attention is split by whole heads. Two conjugate operators (f, g) insert exactly two all-reduces in the forward pass and two in the backward pass per layer — that low, fixed communication cost is what makes tp practical. Crucially for a memory budget, only the split region divides by the tp degree; layer norm, dropout, and residuals are duplicated on every GPU. The authors compose 8-way tp with 64-way data parallelism to reach 512 GPUs at 76% scaling efficiency.
coreIdeas: The MLP splits column-parallel (first GEMM) then row-parallel (second GEMM) so GeLU runs per-partition with no sync; attention splits by assigning whole heads to GPUs — each GPU runs its heads' softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V locally.
The f and g conjugate operators reduce the whole per-layer communication cost to two all-reduces forward and two backward; tensor parallelism is orthogonal to, and composes with, data parallelism.

Only the tensor-parallel region (GEMM weights, attention heads, their gradients and optimizer state) divides by the tp degree; layer norm, dropout, and residuals are duplicated across GPUs and do not shrink.
megatron-lm-training-multi-billion-param.whyItMatters: This is where Phase 7's tp divisor comes from. To hand-write a correct per-GPU memory-budget calculator you must know precisely which tensors divide by tp and which are replicated — Megatron's split-vs-duplicate distinction is the answer, and its two-all-reduce-per-pass accounting is the communication model your DDP-plus-tensor-parallel drills sit inside.
megatron-lm-training-multi-billion-param.phaseConnection: Use it while building the per-GPU memory-budget calculator: apply the tp divisor only to the split GEMM/attention weights, gradients, and optimizer state (remember Adam's momentum and variance), keep layer norm / dropout / residual replicated, and add activation-checkpointing effects. Then run the DDP drills on the rented multi-GPU node as the orthogonal data-parallel axis Megatron composes with tp.
suggestedReadingFocus: Section 3: why the MLP first GEMM must be column-parallel (nonlinear GeLU) and the second row-parallel, and how attention splits by heads
The f/g operators and Figure 4 — the two-all-reduce-per-pass communication cost of a tensor-parallel layer
What is duplicated vs. split across model-parallel GPUs, and how tp and data parallelism compose to 512 GPUs (Table 1, Figure 5)

zero-memory-optimizations-toward-trainin.oneSentence: ZeRO removes data-parallel memory redundancy by sharding optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across ranks in three cumulative stages, turning per-GPU memory into an exact, tunable accounting problem.
zero-memory-optimizations-toward-trainin.summary: ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) reframes the fit-a-large-model problem as bookkeeping: every training tensor is either a model state (optimizer states, gradients, parameters) or a residual state (activations, temporary buffers, fragmentation), and for mixed-precision Adam the model states total (2+2+K)*Psi = 16*Psi bytes per parameter-set, with K=12 coming from three fp32 tensors — the master parameter copy, momentum, and variance. Standard data parallelism replicates all 16*Psi bytes on every GPU; ZeRO-DP instead partitions them across the N_d ranks in three stages (P_os, P_os+g, P_os+g+p) that shard the optimizer states, then the gradients, then the parameters, driving per-device memory from 16*Psi toward 16*Psi/N_d while communication stays between 1x and 1.5x of baseline. For a curriculum where the learner writes a memory-budget calculator, this paper is the specification.
coreIdeas: Per-device training memory decomposes cleanly into model states (params + gradients + optimizer states) and residual states, and for mixed-precision Adam the model-state cost is (2 + 2 + K)*Psi bytes with K = 12.

The optimizer-state multiplier K = 12 is three fp32 tensors per parameter: an fp32 master weight copy, Adam momentum, and Adam variance — this is the dominant, easily-forgotten term in a memory budget.

A single zero_stage knob controls how much is sharded across N_d ranks: stage 1 divides only the optimizer states by N_d, stage 2 also divides the gradients, stage 3 divides everything (the full 16*Psi) by N_d.
The memory savings are nearly free in communication: stages 1 and 2 match baseline DP's 2*Psi volume, and stage 3 costs only 3*Psi (1.5x) for an N_d-fold memory reduction.
Stage 3 (full parameter sharding with on-demand all-gather and discard) is exactly the full-shard mode that PyTorch FSDP later productized.
zero-memory-optimizations-toward-trainin.whyItMatters: This paper is the literal source of the accounting a Phase 7 learner hand-writes: the per-GPU memory-budget calculator whose zero_stage parameter shards optimizer states (stage 1), gradients (stage 2), and parameters (stage 3) across data-parallel ranks, including the 12-bytes-per-param optimizer-state term for mixed-precision Adam. Getting the calculator right means reproducing Figure 1's numbers (Psi = 7.5B, N_d = 64, K = 12 giving 120 / 31.4 / 16.6 / 1.9 GB) exactly.
zero-memory-optimizations-toward-trainin.phaseConnection: In Phase 7 (distributed training) the learner implements the memory-budget calculator directly from Section 3.1 and Figure 1, then rents a multi-GPU node and runs FSDP — ZeRO-3's descendant — checking the calculator's predictions against nvidia-smi. The residual states from Section 3.2 (activations, temporary buffers, fragmentation) are the reason nvidia-smi reads higher than a model-state-only budget, so the paper also tells the learner where the headroom must go.
suggestedReadingFocus: Section 3.1: the 2*Psi + 2*Psi + K*Psi model-state breakdown and why mixed-precision Adam gives K = 12.
Figure 1 and Section 5.1-5.3: the per-stage memory formulas (4*Psi + K*Psi/N_d; 2*Psi + (2+K)*Psi/N_d; 16*Psi/N_d) and the worked 7.5B / N_d=64 example to reproduce.

Section 7: how much each stage costs in communication (2*Psi, 2*Psi, 3*Psi), i.e. why FSDP full-shard is the standard large-model trade-off, and Section 3.2 for the residual states that explain the gap to nvidia-smi.
